strategies.label: Greet Students at the Door
strategies.summary: Greeting students at the door is one example of an effective entry routine. The goal is not the greeting itself; the goal is creating a predictable transition from the hallway into learning.
solves: Unstructured transition time
Difficulty beginning class
Limited teacher-student connection
Lost instructional minutes
Lack of predictability
mechanism: Predictable routines reduce uncertainty — cognitive load drops
Students receive an immediate cue that learning has begun — attention shifts in
Teachers gather quick information before instruction
Positive interactions strengthen relationships and belonging
Entry becomes intentional rather than accidental
conditions: Students know what to do immediately after entering — routine taught
Bell work or an opening task is already prepared
Materials are accessible
Classroom expectations have been explicitly taught
Teacher can monitor both hallway and classroom

misconception.common: Standing at the door is often presented as best practice.
misconception.principle: Create a predictable, personal transition into learning.

implementations.label: Relational
implementations.description: Teacher greets every student by name and briefly checks in before directing them to the opening task.
best_fit: Teachers who enjoy conversation
Smaller classes

implementations.label: Procedural
implementations.description: Teacher greets students while directing them to begin a posted bell ringer.
best_fit: Teachers emphasizing efficient transitions
Larger classes

implementations.label: Low-Verbal
implementations.description: Teacher stands near the entrance, makes eye contact, smiles or nods, while students independently begin the entry routine.
best_fit: Teachers with quieter personalities
Students who thrive on predictable routines

strategies.label: 2x10
strategies.summary: 2x10 is two minutes of non-academic conversation with one hard-to-reach student, held for ten school days running. The goal is building a durable relationship with a student who is currently reachable only through the deed, not the person.
strategies.attribution: Attributed to Raymond Wlodkowski; later popularized in Allen Mendler's Connecting with Students.
solves: A student who feels unseen or only-seen-when-in-trouble
Redirections that keep spending the bond instead of building it
A relationship that starts and stays in the negative
Escalating behavior with no relational channel to reach through
Limited one-on-one connection during a full teaching day
mechanism: Ten consecutive days signals reliability — the student learns the adult keeps coming back
Non-academic content means the interaction is not about compliance
Repeated positive contact builds relationship before the next hard moment
A felt sense of belonging conditions motivation
The channel engagement and feedback travel on gets stronger
conditions: The conversations stay genuinely non-academic — no schoolwork, no behavior talk
The teacher can protect two low-stakes minutes daily
Consistency across all ten days — a broken streak resets the signal
The teacher is curious about this student, not gathering leverage
The student is not put on the spot publicly

misconception.common: 2x10 is often presented as a behavior-fix trick.
misconception.principle: Build the relationship before you need it, on the student's terms, not the classroom's.

implementations.label: Conversational
implementations.description: Teacher initiates a brief, genuine chat about the student's interests — a game, a show, a weekend — following the student's lead each day.
best_fit: Teachers who connect easily through talk
Students who warm to verbal attention

implementations.label: Low-Verbal
implementations.description: Teacher uses short, repeated micro-contacts: noticing a shirt, a quick shared joke, a saved seat. Two minutes spread across small moments rather than one sit-down.
best_fit: Teachers with quieter styles
Students who find direct one-on-one talk intense

implementations.label: Interest-Anchored
implementations.description: Teacher opens with something from an interest survey or an observed hobby, and returns to that thread daily so the student sees continuity from one day to the next.
best_fit: Teachers who prefer a concrete starting point
Students who take time to trust that attention is real

adaptations: Split the two minutes across two staff who share the student
Written back-and-forth for students who prefer text to talk
Interest survey as a launch point
Extend past ten days when momentum is building
Team version: several teachers each run 2x10 with different students
strategies.evidence_note: Wlodkowski's 85% improvement figure is practitioner-reported and illustrative, not a measured finding.
rp_connections: Relationship built before trouble is what lets correction land later
Naming the deed not the doer

strategies.label: Precorrection
strategies.summary: Precorrection is a brief reminder of the expected steps, given right before a predictable challenge point. The goal is to cue the routine at the seam, before things come apart, so the teacher never has to react after.
solves: Predictable off-task moments at transition seams
Repeated redirection for the same expected step
Time lost re-establishing order after it breaks
Students entering a hard task without a clear first move
A reactive cycle: wait for the misbehavior, then correct it
mechanism: The expected step is active in working memory exactly when it is needed — cognitive load drops at the seam
A specific cue focuses attention on the next action instead of the whole noisy environment
Reminding the routine rehearses it — each precorrection is a low-stakes retrieval that strengthens the pattern
Behavior support becomes proactive: the teacher shapes the moment instead of policing it, which keeps relationships out of a correction posture
conditions: The routine being cued was explicitly taught and practiced
The teacher can anticipate which moments predictably go sideways
The cue is specific and short — the exact next step, not a general reminder to behave
There is time to deliver it before the demand, not in the middle of it
Expectations are stable enough that a brief reminder activates them

misconception.common: Precorrection is often heard as warning students or getting ahead of the bad kids.
misconception.principle: Anticipate the seam, and cue the expected step before the demand arrives.

implementations.label: Verbal, whole-group
implementations.description: Just before a known transition, the teacher names the steps aloud: In a moment we are moving to the carpet. That means push in your chair, walk, and find your spot on the rug. Then the transition begins.
best_fit: Teachers comfortable with clear verbal cues
Whole-class transitions with a shared next step

implementations.label: Visual / signal-based
implementations.description: A posted anchor chart or projected slide shows the steps; the teacher points to it right before the challenge point, letting the visual carry the reminder.
best_fit: Teachers who prefer low-verbal cueing
Early readers, multilingual classrooms, students who anchor on predictable visuals

implementations.label: Individual / quiet
implementations.description: The teacher steps beside a student just before the hard moment and privately previews the next step: When we start independent work, your first move is to open to page 4.
best_fit: Teachers building trust with a student who struggles at a specific seam
Situations where a public reminder would single someone out

adaptations: Pre-task checklist previewed before independent work
Role assignment stated before group work begins
What does this look like — quick student rehearsal before the moment
Precorrective reminder paired with a visual timer
One-line reminder at the top of the board for the day's known pinch point
strategies.evidence_note: Kounin's work on momentum and withitness (1970) established that smooth classrooms anticipate friction at activity boundaries rather than reacting to it.
sol_connections: Specific cue directs Attention to the next action
Working Memory holds the step because it was just activated
rp_connections: Correcting before rather than after keeps relationships out of a discipline frame
Support offered to everyone, not aimed at the usual suspects

strategies.label: Co-Created Norms
strategies.summary: Co-created norms are a class agreement authored with students. The goal is not the list on the wall; the goal is authorship. Students who help write the norms hold them, because they own them. This is where investment replaces compliance.
solves: Expectations that students follow but do not believe
Rules that feel imposed rather than shared
Weak buy-in when a teacher hands down a posted list
Norms that get ignored the moment the teacher looks away
A thin sense of belonging in the room's culture
mechanism: Authorship creates ownership — students hold norms they helped write
Investment replaces compliance: the agreement is theirs, so following it is self-consistency rather than obedience
Autonomy of authorship feeds motivation — voice in the rules raises the will to keep them (SoL Q4)
Shared, predictable expectations reduce extraneous cognitive load — students are not guessing what is allowed
Co-authorship is a pathway to belonging — helping name how the room treats each other is a way of belonging to it
conditions: Student voice is real, not decorative — their words actually make it onto the wall
Norms are few, simple, and positively stated
The agreement is revisited and revised, not signed once and forgotten
Enough relational trust exists that students will speak honestly
The teacher is willing to be bound by the agreement too

misconception.common: Let the students make the rules is often presented as the practice.
misconception.principle: Authorship creates ownership — students hold the norms they helped write.

implementations.label: K-2: Read-Aloud to Values
implementations.description: Teacher reads a picture book about friendship or fairness, then asks how the class wants the room to feel. Student answers become a short anchor chart, illustrated and signed.
best_fit: Early elementary
Teachers who anchor culture in story and image

implementations.label: Upper Elementary: Co-Drafted Agreement
implementations.description: Students brainstorm in small groups, the class clusters ideas into shared expectations, and everyone drafts and signs the agreement. Posted and revisited regularly.
best_fit: Grades 3-5
Teachers who want a durable, student-owned document

implementations.label: Middle School: Discussion of Why
implementations.description: Before writing anything, students discuss why norms matter — what a good room feels like, what erodes it. From that conversation they co-create and commit to the agreement.
best_fit: Grades 6-8
Teachers building motivation through reasoning and voice

adaptations: Group-work agreements for a single project
Norm revisit after a rough week
Restorative circle to author or renew the agreement
Family or home input into the class values
sol_connections: Autonomy of authorship feeds Motivation (SoL Q4)
Predictable expectations reduce extraneous Cognitive Load
Working Memory freed for learning when the room is predictable
rp_connections: Co-created norms shift compliance to investment (Klevan 2021)
